translation:
Moyshe Flichtnraykh, Hersh Leyzer Lande, Meir Leyb Gelernter. The same “Agudat” councilmen were also members of the Jewish community. Moshe Aharon Vayntroib was elected as a deputy to the magistrate. His place as councilman was taken by Shmuel Arie. The representative of the artisans in the town council was Mates Mandelboym, from the right-wing P.Z.—Yaakov Likhtenshtits; from the “Left”—Shlomo Zakalik. The latter was not a councilman for long. The police arrested him, and after spending a year in the Shchedletser prison tower, he fell ill with tuberculosis. He was released, but had to move to Warsaw, where he died a short time later.

In 1928, a four-grade Jewish folk school of “TSYSHO” was opened, with four teachers. The local people of America and the Central School Organization in Warsaw helped support the school. The Polish school authorities granted permission to open the school. The classrooms were large, clean, and comfortable. Children six years old and older were admitted.
translatorNotes: “אגודד” is preserved as the OCR’s apparent form of “Agudat”; the exact organizational name is uncertain.
“מאיאסטראט” is translated as “magistrate,” referring to the municipal authority.
“שעדלעצע ר טורמ ע” is rendered “Shchedletser prison tower”; the place/name reading is uncertain in the OCR.
“צישא” is transliterated “TSYSHO,” the Yiddish school organization acronym.
